_about: Registry for the 'Uses & studies' drawer (site/js/stories.js). Rules: every number or claim in a kind='published' card was verified against the cited PDF in bibliography/ on 2026-10-23; 'verified' records where. Only figures stated in the paper - no percentages or values derived from its tables. kind='explore' cards carry a question only - no numbers, no claims.

stories.question: How unusual was the 2020 lake-level rise?
stories.finding: Lake Victoria rose by 1.21 m in the six months to 17 May 2020, reaching a record 13.46 m on the Jinja gauge - a 63-year event in the current climate, estimated 1.8 times as likely (95% CI 0.8-15.8) than in a pre-industrial climate.
stories.citation: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), Earth System Dynamics 15, 225-264

verified.claim: 1.21 m rise, Nov 2019 - 17 May 2020 (84% of the 1.44 m Sep 2019 - May 2020 rise); 'record-breaking level of 13.46 m measured in situ on 17 May 2020' - the in-situ record is the Jinja gauge (gauge datum, not metres a.s.l., hence 'on the Jinja gauge' in the finding)
verified.where: abstract p.225; sect. 1.1 p.227; in-situ series at Jinja: sect. 2 p.229; sect. 3.3 p.234

stories.caveat: The confidence interval includes 1, so the attribution to climate change is suggestive, not conclusive - the paper says so itself.

stories.question: What drove the 2019-2020 rise?
stories.finding: Satellite gravimetry and altimetry put the rise at ~1.4 m. Rainfall in the September-November 2019 short rains had the dominant effect, and a strong positive Indian Ocean Dipole is identified as the main cause of the above-average rains.

verified.claim: ~1.4 m rise (1.387 m, mid-2020 vs the same time in 2019)
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 4 p.8; conclusions p.16

verified.claim: SON 2019 short rains dominant (MAM 2019 was also above average)
IOD the main driver (precipitation correlation 0.69; ENSO 0.32, NAO 0.27)
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 4.5 p.14; sect. 5 p.15

stories.caveat: This app's short-rains season is October–December; Khaki & Awange used September–November.

stories.question: Who was affected by the 2020 floods?
stories.finding: More than 29,000 people living within 50 km of the shoreline are estimated to have been affected by flooding over 5 Apr–1 Jul 2020, the paper's radar window, over a flooded area of about 642.5 km².
stories.citation: Pietroiusti et al. (2024), Earth System Dynamics 15, 225-264

verified.claim: 'more than 29 000 people... affected by floods between April and July 2020' (exact estimate 29,070, stated for Apr-Jun in table 1); 'affected', not displaced
verified.where: abstract p.225; sect. 3.2 p.232; table 1 p.235

verified.claim: flooded area ~642.5 km² within 50 km of the shores; SAR window 5 April 2020-1 July 2020
verified.where: window: methods sect. 2.1.1 p.228; area: sect. 3.2 p.232, fig. 5 p.237

stories.caveat: Our GFM flood layer agrees only partly with the paper's flood map - see DATA_REPORT §3.1 for where and why. The paper's text also calls this window April–July (sect. 3.2) and April–June (Fig. 5).

stories.question: Where did drought risk change as forest became farmland?
stories.finding: SWAT modelling of the basin under its 1985 versus 2014 land cover shows hydrological drought became more frequent and longer-lasting, particularly in the central-western and eastern basin where forest was massively converted to agricultural land. Agriculture grew from about 35 % to 65 % of the basin over that period; grassland shrank from 30 % to 10 %.

verified.claim: 'hydrological drought was generally aggravated with increased drought frequency and lengthened duration, particularly for the central western and eastern regions with massive conversion of forest to agricultural land'
verified.where: abstract p.1; results p.6 and p.8; conclusions p.9

verified.claim: method: SWAT run with the 1985 and 2014 LULC maps; droughts from the 3-month standardized runoff index (SRI <= -1)
'the agricultural area increased from approximately 35 % in 1985 to 65 % in 2014'; 'the grassland area decreased from 30 % in 1985 to 10 % in 2014'

stories.caveat: The app's SPI-3 shows rainfall deficit; the paper's droughts are runoff droughts (3-month SRI from a model), so the two patterns need not match.

stories.question: How has land use changed across the basin?
stories.finding: Between 1985 and 2014 forests, woodlands, grasslands and wetlands were converted to farmland and settlements: small-scale farmland grew by over 90%, from about 5.7 to 11.0 million hectares, urban areas grew by over 800%, and open grasslands declined by 41%.

verified.claim: conversion of forests, woodlands, grasslands, wetlands to farmlands or settlements, 1985-2014
small-scale farmlands +'over 90%', 5,656,113.81 ha (1985) to 11,016,723.51 ha (2014); urban +'over 800%'; open grasslands -41%; all as printed (no derived shares)

stories.caveat: Indicative change only: the app's land-cover layer (Esri/IO LULC, 2017-) is a different product and period than the paper's Landsat classification (1985-2014).

stories.question: Which sub-catchments supply the Nyando's sediment?
stories.finding: Geochemical fingerprinting of riverbed sediment apportions the Nyando catchment's sediment mixture to the Nyando-Kipchorian (44 ± 4 %) and Ainamutua (39 ± 4 %) sub-catchments - highland areas affected by cropping on steep slopes and deforestation - with 17 ± 7 % from the Awach Kano and Nyaidho.

verified.claim: Nyando-Kipchorian 44 ± 4 %, Ainamutua 39 ± 4 %, Awach Kano and Nyaidho 17 ± 7 % of the Nyando riverbed-sediment end-point mixture
verified.where: abstract p.1; sect. 3.2 p.5, fig. 5a; conclusions p.12

stories.caveat: These are modelled shares of the riverbed sediment sampled within the Nyando basin, not measured sediment flux to Lake Victoria. Rivers are drawn on the map; the Nyando's headwaters are the highlands in view.

stories.question: Could the app show water quality in the lake?
stories.finding: Chlorophyll-a and turbidity algorithms for Sentinel-2 can be aligned with Sentinel-3 so the two sensors give complementary observations, and Lake Victoria is among the 24 lakes tuned. But the study is satellite-to-satellite: no in-situ measurements were used for any lake, Lake Victoria included.
stories.citation: Warren et al. (2021), Remote Sensing of Environment 265, 112651

verified.claim: MSI tuned against OLCI; complementary chl-a and turbidity observations; Lake Victoria one of 24 study lakes
verified.where: abstract p.1; table 1 p.3; figs. 9-10 p.12; conclusions p.15

verified.claim: no in-situ validation data for any lake ('large in situ data gaps... prevent direct calibration and validation')

stories.caveat: Not in the app yet: a water-quality layer would need this kind of retrieval plus field checks on Lake Victoria.

stories.question: Where do fires cluster, and in which season?
stories.caveat: No fire study of the basin is in bibliography/ yet - use the layer's year control to look for patterns.

stories.question: How much land burns in a typical year?
stories.caveat: No burned-area study of the basin is in bibliography/ yet - the layer's annual totals are a starting point.
